messages.subject: hierarchical mixture modelling
parts:
Hi folks,

I'm trying to implement a hierarchical mixture model and I was hoping
to get some help with a few sticking points I've encountered thus far.
I've created a gist (https://gist.github.com/3734783) that has R code
for explaining/generating the data that I'm attempting to model. The
gist also has my attempt thus far at coding the stan model.


2 Technical questions:

1) How would I go about defining the VonMises distribution for use in
Stan? (In R, I just use the rvm() and dvm() functions from the
CircStats package.)

2) Does it look like I implemented the mixture appropriately? I tried
to understand and extend the mixture example from the docs, but I
might have missed something.


And a more theory-related question:

So far the data-generating R code and stan fitting code assumes zero
covariance amongst the three parameters that get sampled per "person"
("person_rho", "person_mu", "person_kappa"). Sampling of person_rho
and person_kappa are both from Gaussians, so I could use
multi_normal() as illustrated in the docs to estimate the covariance
between these parameters. However, where person_mu is sampled from a
VonMises, I'm guessing there's no way to simultaneously estimate all 3
covariances? In this case, I guess I could still use multi_normal() to
estimate the covariance between person_rho and person_kappa, then
simply assume that the other 2 covariances are zero (coincidentally,
I'm not *as* interested in those covariances anyway). However, I
wonder if I should be concerned about any influence on the accuracy of
inference this assumption might have if it is violated by the data.
Thoughts?

Another solution might be to give up use of the Von Mises for
representing the distribution of person_mu values; my data is unlikely
to have dramatic variability in person_mu values (they're likely all
pretty close to zero), so I suspect I could get away with using a
Gaussian. Though presumably in this case I'd still need to ensure that
the sampled person_mu values are constrained to the finite range (-pi
to pi) that mu can take, which I'm guessing might be achieved by
sampling the Gaussian on the real then transforming the result
(something like: inverse_logit(sample)*2*pi-pi ). In this case,
however, I'm not sure how to extend the docs example of using
multi_normal() in the 2-parameter case to the 3-parameter case;
specifically, do I need to do anything to ensure that sigma is
positive definite?

Thanks to anyone who suffered through this long post,

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hierarchical mixture modelling
parts:
The model looks pretty close to what you'd need.

Just a couple of sticking points in the loop:

real ps[2];
for (t in 1:T) {
ps[1] <- log(person_rho) + log(vonMises(person_mu,person_kappa));
ps[2] <- log(1-person_rho) + log(uniform(-pi(),pi()));
lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(ps);

First, you want to replace the term

log(uniform(-pi(),pi()))

with

uniform_log(person_mu, -pi(), pi());

The notation uniform(L,H) is for when there is a sampling
statement, as in:

person_mu ~ uniform(-pi(), pi());

This just translates into a form that calls the three-argument
uniform_log() function.

Next, you can eliminate the ps[2] local variable and just
use the binary log_sum_exp function and simplify the loop to:

for (t in 1:T) {
lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log(person_rho) + log(vonMises(person_mu,person_kappa)),
log(1-person_rho) + uniform_log(person_mu,-pi(),pi()));

But person_mu isn't constrained to lie in (-pi, pi) in the model,
and if it's a mixture of von Mises and uniform, the uniform needs
to have all of the person_mu in its support or you'll get an error
when evaluating the uniform_log.

Now as for how to do the von Mises, that looks a bit
sticky, because there's a (log) Bessel function of
order 0 that depends on the concentration parameter:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Mises_distribution

Now if we had Bessel functions available in Stan, you could
code the distribution as with the mixture by incrementing
the log probability accumulator lp__ appropriately. Or if
the concentration parameters were constant, you could do
the same but drop the Bessel term.

What we would need to do to support Bessel functions would
be to write a C++ implementation of the function and its
derivative. I think we'd just need order 0 and order 1
functions. Looks like Boost provides a generic implementation
for any order, so it shouldn't actually be too hard:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_51_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/special/bessel/bessel.html

I'll add it to our function to-do list. Maybe someone will
take it up sooner rather than later.

By the way, this is also what we'd need to add the
von Mises distribution to Stan, which would save you the
work of coding its density.

- Bob

On Tue, Sep 18, 2012 at 2:05 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I was talking to Michael Betancourt today who said
> that we'd also have problems with HMC on the
> von Mises distro because of the way it wraps -- there's
> no way to unconstrain and retain the locality probperties
> in R^N.

In practice I expect that if you left the von Mises distributed
parameter unconstrained but evaluated it mod 2pi there wouldn't be any
issues. Technically, this produces an improper distribution over R
but I don't think it would cause a real problem.

That said, distributions like the von Mises are one big motivation to
implement a version of NUTS with nonlinear parameter constraints.

Cheers,
Marcus

Does this apply to models that (1) use a Von Mises as the data
distribution, (2) use the Von Mises as a distribution of
hyperparameters, or both?

As I noted earlier, with my data, I expect that most of the
hyperparameter values specifying the VonMises location are going to be
pretty close to zero, so I could replace the Von Mises there with a
Gaussian (truncated or on a transformed scale that accounts for the
-pi to pi bounds).

If the problem applies to using Von Mises as the data distribution,
then this is more troublesome. Though I'm now thinking that my data is
also likely to have pretty high values for the concentration
parameter, so a uniform-plus-truncated-Gaussian mixture for the data
distribution might be an ok approximation to the
uniform-plus-VonMises. Since this is already possible in stan, I'll
give this a shot later today and see how things go.

Note that acos : [-1,1] -> [0,pi] not -> [-pi,pi] so the range of x is
limited. It also doesn't allow users to write x~vonMises(u,k) where x
is an angle because the transform is not generic on x, but is
dependent on the distribution parameter u.

To be clear the issue with the other obvious solution of constraining
x to be in [-pi,pi] is that it breaks the space such that transitions
from +pi to -pi are practically impossible with a general purpose
sampler like HMC/NUTS.

Cheers,

How about we map the random variable to two dimensions? I.e., do something like

parameters {
real x;
real y;
}
transformed parameters {
real phi;
real z;
phi <- atan2(x, y);
z <- x*x + y*y;
}
model {
phi ~ von_mises(mu, kappa);
z ~ gamma(0.5, 0.5);
}

The resulting pdf in x-y space is unimodal, which should be a lot
easier to deal with than sampling on the original (-pi, pi) space.

If you're not committed to the Von Mises distributional form, you
could do something easier, like say

parameters {
real x;
real y;
}
transformed parameters {
real phi;
phi <- atan2(x, y);
}
model {
x ~ normal(kappa * cos(mu), 1);
y ~ normal(kappa * sin(mu), 1);
}

which will likewise express the idea that phi should be close to mu,
with a circular variance that goes down as kappa goes up.

Matt

The error message is correct -- when you write multi_normal(mu,sigma)
on the right side of an assignment, it tries to find a binary
function called multi_normal(), which doesn't exist.

I'm guessing that what you're trying to do is generate a
random sample from a multivariate normal with mean mu and
covar matrix sigma. Stan doesn't support that and won't wind
up supporting it in models because it loses the gradient
connection.

Instead, you'll have to define mv_sample as a parameter (not
a transformed parameter) and write the following:

mv_sample ~ multi_normal(mu,sigma);

With that change, the model will look like:

data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> T;
real<lower=-pi(),upper=pi()> y[N,T];
}
parameters {

vector[3] mu;
cov_matrix[3] sigma;
vector[3] mv_sample;
}
model {
for (n in 1:N) {
mv_sample ~ multi_normal(mu,sigma);

for (t in 1:T) {
lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(
log(

inv_logit(mv_sample[1])) +
normal_log(y[n,t],mv_sample[2],sqrt(exp(mv_sample[3]))
) ,
log1m(
inv_logit(mv_sample[1])) +
uniform_log(y[n,t],-pi(),pi()
)
);
}
}
}

I also replaced log(1 - x) in the second log_sum_exp term with
the more arithmetically stable log1m(x).

In terms of style, I would recommend:

lp__ <- lp__
+ log_sum_exp(log(inv_logit(mv_sample[1]))
+ normal_log(y[n,t],
mv_sample[2],
sqrt(exp(mv_sample[3]))),
log1m(inv_logit(mv_sample[1])) +
uniform_log(y[n,t],-pi(),pi())));

Also, you can precompute things like sqrt(exp(mv_sample[3])) out of
the loop for t and reuse the value.

- Bob

The default prior is always uniform over the support of the parameter.

and similarly the priors for the correlation matrix is uniform
between -1 and 1 for each correlation, correct?

This is a subtle but important misstatement: That prior for the correlation matrix is jointly uniform over KxK correlation matrices (symmetric, PSD, unit diagonal). If the prior were marginally uniform on [-1,1] for each of the K choose 2 correlations, then there would be a (large) region of the parameter space where the correlation matrix was not PSD. A mostly irrelevant fact is that under a jointly uniform prior, the marginal correlations are all scale-and-shifts of a symmetric beta distribution to the [-1,1] interval.

While I actually don't really have any more informative priors in my head for my data, I do
wonder what I should do in the future if I wanted non-uniform priors implemented.

At the moment, Stan doesn't have many great options for priors on a univariate parameter with bounded support on both sides. We should probably have a generalization of the beta distribution for these situations with a minimum, maximum, mean, and dispersion.

Stan supports an informative prior over a correlation matrix with the lkj_corr(eta) distribution. If eta == 1.0, the distribution is jointly uniform, so it is a (big) waste of time and RAM to call it. But you can choose eta to be something other than 1.0; in particular to the extent that eta is greater than 1.0, the lkj prior has a sharper mode at the identity matrix.
